summary: Defines requirements for IPv6 nodes, so IPv6 works well and interoperates across many devices and deployments. It is Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 6434, and in turn RFC 4294.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of the IPv6 features that devices should have, and how strongly each one is recommended. It covers everything from the lowest network layer up to name lookup and security, so that a device built from the list works with the rest of the Internet.

subtitle: A single checklist of which IPv6 specifications a host or router should implement, and at what level.

tldr.problem: IPv6 is spread over many separate specifications, and the makers of hosts, routers and small devices need to know which of them matter for the Internet to work.
tldr.mechanism: The document is an applicability statement. It walks through the layers of the stack and marks each referenced specification as MUST, SHOULD or MAY, without redefining any of the protocols.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6434 and sets out a minimal baseline for useful Internet service, while leaving room for stricter profiles for particular deployments. The overriding rule is Postel's Robustness Principle: be conservative in what you do and liberal in what you accept.

today: RFC 8504 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 220) published in January 2019. It obsoletes RFC 6434, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Is For
sections.content:
The document defines common functionality required by both IPv6 hosts and IPv6 routers. It borrows its definitions from RFC 8200: an IPv6 node is a device that implements IPv6, an IPv6 router is a node that forwards IPv6 packets not explicitly addressed to itself, and an IPv6 host is any IPv6 node that is not a router.

The document is an applicability statement: it collects requirements from other Standards Track documents in one place and avoids protocol detail. It does not update any individual protocol RFC.

The requirements are a minimal level needed for a device to provide useful Internet service, and the wide range of deployment scenarios means they may not be sufficient for all of them. It is perfectly reasonable, and expected, for other profiles to define additional or stricter requirements for particular environments. As an example, this document does not mandate that all clients support DHCP, but some deployment scenarios may deem it appropriate. NIST has defined profiles for specialised requirements for IPv6 in target environments.

As it is not always possible for an implementer to know the exact usage of IPv6 in a node, an overriding requirement is that nodes adhere to Jon Postel's Robustness Principle: be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a checklist, not a design. It collects in one place what other standards say, so a device maker knows which features to include for the device to work with everyone else's.

sections.title: How to Read the Requirements
sections.content:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, NOT RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14, RFC 2119 and RFC 8174, when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

An IPv6 node must include support for one or more IPv6 link-layer specifications, and which ones it should include depends on the link layers supported by the hardware available on the system. It is possible for a conformant IPv6 node to support IPv6 on some of its interfaces and not on others. The document lists link layers for which an IPv6 specification has been developed, for information only: transmission over Ethernet, Frame Relay, IEEE 1394, Fibre Channel, IEEE 802.15.4, IEEE 802.16 and PPP, and tunnelling such as Teredo and the basic transition mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: MUST means you cannot skip it, SHOULD means skip it only with a good reason, and MAY means it is your choice. At the bottom, a device has to work over at least one kind of network link.

sections.title: The IP Layer and Extension Headers
sections.content:
Support for RFC 8200 is a MUST and the node must follow the packet transmission rules in it. All conformant implementations must be able to send and receive IPv6 packets; forwarding functionality may be supported. Nodes must always be able to send, receive and process Fragment headers, must not create overlapping fragments, and when reassembling a datagram that contains an overlapping fragment the entire datagram and any constituent fragments must be silently discarded. Nodes must not generate atomic fragments, and should avoid predictable Fragment Identification values. All nodes should support setting and using the IPv6 Flow Label field.

An IPv6 node must be able to process the extension headers, with one exception: Routing Header type 0, which was deprecated for security reasons, must be treated as an unrecognized routing type. When a node fragments a datagram it must include the entire IPv6 header chain in the first fragment. Defining new extension headers is not recommended unless no existing extension header can be used by specifying a new option for it.

Because the only limit on the number and size of extension headers is the MTU, a long chain could be used as a denial-of-service attack, so a host may place limits on what it is willing to process. A host may limit consecutive PAD1 options to 7, may limit the bytes in a PADN option to less than 8, may disallow unknown options, and may impose a limit on the maximum number of non-padding options, where the maximum should be configurable and the default should be 8. A host may also impose a limit on the maximum length of the Destination Options or Hop-by-Hop Options extension headers, where the default is to accept options of any length. Packets that exceed a limit should be silently discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A device has to be able to unpack any of the optional headers an IPv6 packet may carry, but it may also refuse packets that carry an unreasonable number of them, since that could be used to overload it.

sections.title: Neighbour Discovery and Related Protocols
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery must be supported. Hosts must support Router Discovery and Prefix Discovery, and must implement Neighbor Unreachability Detection for all paths between hosts and neighbouring nodes. Hosts must support sending Router Solicitations and receiving Router Advertisements. All nodes must support sending and receiving Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages, which Duplicate Address Detection requires. Hosts should support processing Redirects, and routers must support sending them, with the sending of Redirects disabled by default on routers intended for core networks. Nodes must not use IPv6 fragmentation for sending Neighbor Discovery and SEcure Neighbor Discovery messages, and must silently ignore such messages on receipt if fragmented.

SEcure Neighbor Discovery has had relatively few implementations in common operating systems since its publication in 2005, so deployment experience remains very limited, and support for it is considered optional.

Path MTU Discovery should be supported, though a minimal implementation may simply restrict itself to sending packets no larger than 1280 octets. Path MTU Discovery relies on ICMPv6 Packet Too Big, and these messages must not be filtered, because blocking them can produce black-hole connections in which a connection completes its handshake and then hangs. ICMPv6 must be supported.

Nodes must implement RFC 4191 for default router preferences and more-specific routes, and should implement the Type C host role. Nodes that need to join multicast groups must support MLDv2, because participation of any MLDv1-only node on a link requires all other nodes on the link to operate in version 1 compatibility mode; source-specific multicast also requires MLDv2. Nodes should support ECN, and an ECN-aware router sets a mark in the IP header to signal impending congestion rather than dropping a packet, which the receiver echoes to the sender so it can reduce its rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices must find each other, find the router, and check that the router is still there. The one thing they must never do is block the message that says a packet was too big for the road, because that turns into connections that hang.

sections.title: Addresses and Address Configuration
sections.content:
The IPv6 Addressing Architecture must be supported, and the current architecture is based on a 64-bit boundary for subnet prefixes. Implementations must also support the multicast flag updates of RFC 7371.

Hosts must support Stateless Address Autoconfiguration. It is RECOMMENDED that, unless there is a specific requirement for MAC addresses to be embedded in the interface identifier, nodes follow the procedure in RFC 7217 to generate SLAAC-based addresses. Addresses generated that way are the same whenever a given device reappears on the same subnet, but the interface identifier varies on each subnet visited. All nodes must implement Duplicate Address Detection, which must be performed on all unicast addresses prior to assigning them to an interface regardless of whether they come from stateless autoconfiguration, DHCPv6 or manual configuration.

Privacy Extensions should be supported, because a node whose address embeds its MAC address keeps the same interface identifier on every network it visits, which lets a third party track it. Devices must provide a way for the end user to explicitly enable or disable the use of temporary addresses. All hosts should implement address configuration via DHCPv6, and DHCPv6 client anonymity profiles should be supported where devices are likely to be carried between networks. The rules of RFC 6724 for default address selection must be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: A device must be able to give itself an address, must check that nobody else on the network has the same one, and must let the user turn on an address that changes from network to network.

sections.title: Name Lookup, Other Configuration and Management
sections.content:
Not all nodes will need to resolve names, but the ability to resolve names is a basic infrastructure capability on which applications rely, so all nodes should implement stub-resolver functionality with support for AAAA type resource records, reverse addressing in ip6.arpa using PTR records, and EDNS(0) to allow DNS packet sizes larger than 512 octets. Those nodes are RECOMMENDED to support the DNS security extensions.

DHCP can also carry configuration that is not an address. If a host implementation supports applications or other protocols that require configuration only available via DHCP, hosts should implement DHCP, and if a node implements DHCP it must implement the DNS options, as most deployments will expect them to be available. There is no defined DHCPv6 Gateway option, so nodes using DHCPv6 are expected to determine their default router and on-link prefix information from received Router Advertisements. Implementations must include support for the DNS Router Advertisement option of RFC 8106, since few nodes can function adequately without a working DNS resolver.

Multicast DNS and DNS-based Service Discovery should be supported where service discovery would be beneficial, for example where users seek to discover printers or display devices. Network management may be supported by IPv6 nodes, though for embedded devices it may be the only way to control them; SNMP, NETCONF and RESTCONF are the existing management protocols, with two MIB modules and two YANG data models marked as SHOULD for the agents that use them.
sections.plainLanguage: A device has to be able to look up names, and it has to learn the address of its router and of the name server. Where a device is small and has no screen, network management may be the only way to configure it at all.

sections.title: Coexistence, Applications, Routers and Small Devices
sections.content:
IPv6 nodes may support IPv4. If a node implements dual stack and tunnelling, RFC 4213 must be supported. Software that allows users and operators to input IPv6 addresses in text form should support the recommended textual representation of RFC 5952. The document does not mandate the use of any particular socket API, because the choice of API does not directly relate to on-the-wire behaviour, but it points to the basic and advanced IPv6 socket APIs and to APIs for source address selection, multicast source filters and Mobile IPv6.

On mobility, Mobile IPv6 has seen only limited implementation and no significant deployment, partly because it originally assumed an IPv6-only environment rather than a mixed IPv4 and IPv6 Internet. More usage and deployment experience is needed before any specific approach can be recommended for broad implementation, so Mobile IPv6 and its associated standards are considered a MAY.

Routers must send Router Advertisements and process Router Solicitations, and forwarding nodes must conform to BCP 198. Routers must support sending Redirects, and a DHCPv6 server function on a router is optional, though routers in complex networks should support relay agents.

For constrained nodes with limited CPU, memory, bandwidth or power, the requirements of this document are RECOMMENDED for all nodes but compromises may be needed. Where compromises are made, interoperability should be strongly considered, particularly where this may affect other nodes on the same link, for example that supporting only MLDv1 affects other nodes. IPv6 nodes that are battery powered should implement the recommendations of RFC 7772.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new address systems can run side by side, and a device may use both. A tiny battery sensor may not manage everything on the list, but it must not break the rules for the other devices on the same network.

sections.title: Security and the Algorithms to Use
sections.content:
Achieving security in practice is a complex undertaking: operational procedures, protocols, key distribution mechanisms and certificate management approaches all affect the level of security actually achieved, and a poor fit in any one component can reduce the overall effectiveness of an approach.

IPsec can provide either end-to-end security between nodes or channel security, in tunnel mode or transport mode. Although IPsec can be used with manual keying in some cases, such usage has limited applicability and is not recommended. A range of security technologies proliferate today, and no single approach has emerged as ideal for all needs; IPsec is not viewed as ideal in all cases and is unlikely to displace the others.

Previously IPv6 mandated implementation of IPsec and recommended the key-management approach of IKE. RFC 6434 updated that recommendation by making support of the IPsec architecture a SHOULD for all IPv6 nodes, and this document retains that recommendation. The IPsec Architecture requires both manual and automatic key management, and the recommended automated key-management protocol to implement is IKEv2. IPv6 nodes implementing the IPsec Architecture must implement ESP and may implement AH, and must conform to the algorithm requirements of RFC 8221, allowing for migration to new algorithms as that document is replaced or updated. Nodes implementing IKEv2 must conform to RFC 8247 or any future update to it.

The document recognises device types where other approaches to security can be justified, such as special-purpose devices supporting only a very limited number of applications, and devices running on extremely constrained hardware such as sensors where the full IPsec Architecture is not justified. Because most common platforms now support IPv6 and have it enabled by default, IPv6 security is an issue for networks that are ostensibly IPv4 only, for which RFC 7123 gives guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule that every IPv6 device must have IPsec was relaxed to a recommendation, and the document says why: one lock does not suit every door, and a sensor on a battery does not need a bank vault.

items.label: IPsec architecture
items.desc: Support for it is a SHOULD, as in RFC 6434.

items.title: Router Discovery
items.text: Hosts must support it, to find routers on the attached link.

items.title: Prefix Discovery
items.text: Hosts must support it, to learn which destinations are on-link.

items.title: Neighbor Unreachability Detection
items.text: Hosts must implement it for all paths to neighbouring nodes.

items.title: Router Solicitations
items.text: Hosts must send them and receive Router Advertisements.

items.title: Solicitation and Advertisement
items.text: All nodes must send and receive them, for Duplicate Address Detection.

items.title: Redirects
items.text: Hosts should process them; routers must send them.
